sections.b: In Jubilees 10 the spirits of the giants lead Noah's grandsons astray. Noah prays and God orders them bound. Then "the chief of the spirits, Mastema," asks that some be left to him, "for the evil of humankind is great." God leaves him a tenth, and the angels leave them "to serve before Satan on the earth" (Jubilees 10:8-11). Jubilees uses Mastema and Satan for the same figure.

sections.h: Jubilees: angels sent to teach, then fallen
sections.b: Jubilees calls the sons of God of Genesis 6:2 "the angels of the Lord" (Jubilees 5:1) and later "the Watchers" (Jubilees 7:21). They had come down to teach humankind (Jubilees 4:15) but took wives. The angels of the presence bound them "in the depths of the earth" (Jubilees 5:6), and their sons, the giants, were made to kill one another (Jubilees 5:7-9). Their spirits became the demons that troubled Noah's family (Jubilees 10:1-6), a tenth of which God left under Mastema.
sections.refs: Jubilees 5:1-10; Jubilees 7:21-25; Jubilees 10:1-11; Genesis 6:1-4; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4

uncommon: Jubilees teaches that the Watchers first came down for a good purpose, to teach humankind and do justice, and fell only after they arrived (Jubilees 4:15; 5:1).

sections.b: In Jubilees the angels' children "were giants" (Jubilees 5:1). Noah names them the Naphidim, the Ge'ez form of Nephilim, and gives three kinds that killed one another in turn, as in the Greek of 1 Enoch 7 (Jubilees 7:22). They did not drown: God sent the sword among them (Jubilees 5:7-9), and their spirits lived on as demons (Jubilees 10:5).
sections.refs: Jubilees 5:1; Jubilees 5:7-10; Jubilees 7:22-24; Jubilees 10:5; Genesis 6:4; Numbers 13:33

sections.h: The Flood in Jubilees: dates and a 364-day year
sections.b: Jubilees retells Genesis 6-8 with exact dates: Noah goes in from the first to the sixteenth of the second month, the Lord shuts the ark on the seventeenth, the ark rests on Mount Lubar, and the earth is dry on the seventeenth of the second month the next year (Jubilees 5:23-31). The four quarter days of its calendar are each tied to a moment of the Flood (Jubilees 6:23-27). Charles reported B. W. Bacon's argument that the Flood dates of Genesis already fit a solar year.

sections.h: Noah in Jubilees: priest, lawgiver, healer
sections.b: Jubilees makes Noah a priest who atones for the earth and offers the Temple's sacrifices (Jubilees 6:1-3), a lawgiver who teaches his grandsons justice, modesty, honor of parents and the ban on blood (Jubilees 7:20-39), the father who divides the earth by lot (Jubilees 8:10-9:15), and a healer who writes down the cures an angel taught him and hands his books to Shem (Jubilees 10:10-14). Charles thought 2 Peter 2:5, "a herald of righteousness," knew Noah's speech in Jubilees 7.

sections.h: Jubilees 6: the year as a law
sections.b: Jubilees turns the 364-day year into a command given to Moses (Jubilees 6:32), with four quarters of thirteen weeks (Jubilees 6:29) and four "days of remembrance" on the first days of months 1, 4, 7 and 10 (Jubilees 6:23). It condemns setting the months by the moon, which "comes ten days early, year after year" (Jubilees 6:36), and warns that a wrong count makes holy days common (Jubilees 6:37). Grintz notes that the Beta Israel of Ethiopia based their calendar, especially the date of Shavuot, on Jubilees.
sections.refs: Jubilees 6:23-38; Jubilees 2:9; Genesis 1:14; Psalm 104:19; Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16

sections.h: Jubilees: the feast of covenant renewal
sections.b: Jubilees makes the Feast of Weeks the yearly renewal of the covenant with Noah, kept in heaven since creation, by Noah's family until his death, then by Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and restored at Sinai (Jubilees 6:17-22). It is "double": the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Firstfruits (Jubilees 6:21). Charles noted that Jubilees never calls it Pentecost.

sections.h: The blood law given to Noah (Jubilees 6-7)
sections.b: Jubilees builds Genesis 9:4-6 into a full law: Noah and his sons swear not to eat blood (Jubilees 6:10), Israel renews the oath at Sinai with sprinkled blood (Jubilees 6:11), and whoever eats blood "will be rooted out of the land" (Jubilees 6:12). Noah adds that the blood of animals must be covered and that only the murderer's blood cleanses the earth (Jubilees 7:28-33).
sections.refs: Jubilees 6:7-14; Jubilees 7:27-33; Genesis 9:4-6; Leviticus 17:10-14; Numbers 35:33; Acts 15:20

sections.b: Jubilees turns Genesis 10 into a map. Noah's sons draw lots from his robe with an angel present: Shem gets the middle of the earth, Ham the hot south, Japheth the cold north (Jubilees 8:10-30). Each son divides his portion among his own sons (Jubilees 9:1-13), and all swear an oath under a curse never to take another's lot (Jubilees 9:14-15). Canaan breaks it (Jubilees 10:29-34). Jubilees also has the extra generation Kainam (Cainan) between Arpachshad and Shelah, as in Luke 3:36 (Jubilees 8:1).

Jubilees dates the tower: the builders bake bricks and build for forty-three years, aiming to "go up by it into heaven" (Jubilees 10:19-21). God speaks to his angels, "Come, let us go down," and they go down with him (Jubilees 10:22-23). After the languages are mixed up, a wind throws the tower down, and the place is called "Overthrow" (Jubilees 10:26). Charles calls the wind "a very old tradition," found also in the Sibylline Oracles and Josephus.

In Jubilees the land "from Lebanon to the Brook of Egypt" fell by lot to Shem (Jubilees 8:12-21). Canaan, whose lot was in the far west, settled there anyway, breaking the oath, and the land was named after him (Jubilees 10:29-34). Charles saw the story as an answer to objections to Israel's conquest: Israel took back what was Shem's. Genesis 15:16 and Leviticus 18:24-28 give a different reason, the sins of the land's people.

In Jubilees an angel (Raphael, says the medieval Hebrew Book of Noah, as Charles reports) teaches Noah the cures for the diseases caused by evil spirits, "so that he could heal with the plants of the earth." Noah writes them in a book and gives it to Shem (Jubilees 10:10-14).

sections.h: Eden as the Holy of Holies (Jubilees 8)
sections.b: Jubilees places Eden in the east, inside Shem's portion, and calls it "the Holy of Holies and the dwelling of the Lord," one of three holy places with Sinai and Zion, "facing one another" (Jubilees 8:16-19).
In Jubilees 10 the chief of the evil spirits is Mastema, and the tenth of the spirits left on earth "serve before Satan on the earth" (Jubilees 10:11). See Mastema.

Noah keeps and teaches the law of Leviticus 19:23-25: three years without picking, the fourth year's fruit holy, its first part offered on the altar and the rest eaten by the priests, and the fifth year "released" (Jubilees 7:1-2, 35-37). Charles notes that later Jewish law gave the fourth-year fruit to the owner instead.
